params.question: Which of the following mechanisms most accurately explains how iron deficiency causes anaemia in children?

answers.text: Accelerated destruction of red blood cells in the spleen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes haemolytic anaemia, where RBC survival is shortened. Iron deficiency impairs red cell production, not destruction.

answers.text: Impaired erythropoiesis due to substrate shortage for haemoglobin synthesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Iron is an essential substrate for haemoglobin synthesis; its deficiency impairs erythropoiesis, placing it squarely under the 'decreased RBC production' mechanism.

answers.text: Chronic occult blood loss from the gastrointestinal tract

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While GI blood loss can cause iron deficiency, the mechanism by which iron deficiency itself produces anaemia is impaired production, not blood loss.
This describes the mechanism of anaemia of chronic disease, where inflammation upregulates hepcidin to trap iron in reticuloendothelial stores — a distinct entity from nutritional iron deficiency.

overallFeedback.feedback: Iron deficiency causes anaemia through impaired erythropoiesis (decreased RBC production) due to substrate shortage — it belongs to the hypoproliferative category, not the haemolytic or blood-loss mechanisms.
Iron deficiency is a classic example of the 'decreased RBC production' (hypoproliferative) mechanism — without adequate iron substrate, the marrow cannot synthesise sufficient haemoglobin.

interactions.label: In megaloblastic anaemia, neurological features such as developmental regression

params.question: In megaloblastic anaemia, neurological features such as developmental regression and hypotonia occur in both vitamin B12 and folate deficiency.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Both B12 and folate deficiency produce identical haematological features (severe pallor, macrocytosis, pancytopenia), but neurological dysfunction is exclusive to B12 deficiency. This distinction is clinically critical: treating a B12-deficient patient with folate alone corrects the anaemia but allows irreversible neurological damage to progress.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. Neurological features — developmental regression, hypotonia, posterior column signs — are specific to vitamin B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency produces identical haematological features (severe pallor, macrocytosis) but spares the nervous system.

interactions.label: A 5-year-old child presents with sudden-onset petechiae and purpura over the leg

params.question: A 5-year-old child presents with sudden-onset petechiae and purpura over the legs. The child is afebrile, active, and playful. Which clinical finding, if present, should immediately shift suspicion away from ITP towards acute lymphoblastic leukaemia?

answers.text: History of a preceding upper respiratory tract infection two weeks ago

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A preceding viral illness is actually a classic feature of ITP — post-viral immune dysregulation triggers antiplatelet antibodies. Its presence supports, rather than argues against, ITP.
Bruising alongside petechiae and purpura is typical of severe thrombocytopenia from any cause, including ITP. It does not by itself distinguish ITP from leukaemia.

Correct. In ITP the child is otherwise completely well — no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no pallor. Hepatosplenomegaly indicates an infiltrative process and mandates exclusion of ALL before attributing thrombocytopenia to ITP.

answers.text: Isolated thrombocytopenia with normal haemoglobin and WBC count

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal haemoglobin and white cell count actually supports ITP. In leukaemia, cytopenias across multiple lineages are expected.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hepatosplenomegaly is the critical red flag. ITP presents in a well child with no organomegaly; its presence should immediately raise suspicion of an infiltrative process such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
The hallmark of ITP is a well child with isolated thrombocytopenia. Any systemic finding — especially hepatosplenomegaly — demands exclusion of malignancy before attributing the picture to ITP alone.

interactions.label: Which pair of pathological processes best explains the full clinical presentatio

params.question: Which pair of pathological processes best explains the full clinical presentation of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in children?

answers.text: Autoimmune platelet destruction and secondary splenic sequestration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pair describes the mechanism of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). In ALL, thrombocytopenia results from marrow replacement by blasts, not autoimmune destruction.

answers.text: Replacement of normal haematopoiesis by malignant blasts and extramedullary infiltration by leukaemic cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Marrow replacement produces the triad of anaemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia, while extramedullary infiltration causes hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and distant organ involvement.

answers.text: Nutritional substrate deficiency and chronic gastrointestinal blood loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are causes of iron deficiency anaemia, not leukaemia. ALL results from clonal proliferation of malignant lymphoid precursors, not substrate deficiency.

answers.text: Excessive hepcidin production and progressive bone marrow fibrosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration occurs in anaemia of chronic disease. Bone marrow fibrosis characterises myelofibrosis — a myeloproliferative neoplasm distinct from ALL.

overallFeedback.feedback: ALL presents through two simultaneous processes: expanding blasts replace normal haematopoiesis (causing anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), and leukaemic cells infiltrate extramedullary organs (causing hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and CNS or testicular involvement).
Understanding this dual mechanism — marrow failure plus extramedullary infiltration — allows you to predict the entire symptom complex of ALL, from cytopenias to organomegaly to bone pain.

interactions.label: A 2-year-old child's CBC is reported using adult reference ranges, and the haemo

params.question: A 2-year-old child's CBC is reported using adult reference ranges, and the haemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL is flagged as 'normal.' What is the most dangerous consequence of this practice?

answers.text: All parameters will be falsely flagged as abnormal, triggering unnecessary investigations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not all paediatric values differ from adult ranges. The greater danger is the opposite — true pathology being missed because the adult range is more permissive for certain parameters.

answers.text: The truly anaemic child may be classified as normal, delaying diagnosis and treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The age-specific threshold for anaemia in children under 5 years is 11 g/dL. At 10.5 g/dL this child is anaemic, but adult ranges may not flag it — delaying evaluation of a potentially serious underlying cause.

answers.text: The white cell differential will be misread because children have physiological lymphocyte predominance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While lymphocyte predominance is physiological in young children and can cause interpretive confusion, the narration emphasises that the most dangerous consequence is a missed diagnosis of true pathology.

answers.text: The laboratory will need to repeat the sample using a paediatric-specific analyser

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The same haematology analyser processes both adult and paediatric samples. Reference range selection is an interpretive decision applied after analysis, not an analytical requirement.

overallFeedback.feedback: The greatest danger is a missed diagnosis: adult cut-offs may classify a truly anaemic child as normal, because paediatric thresholds for children under 5 years are higher than adult lower limits.

Applying adult reference ranges to a child's CBC can mask true pathology — an anaemic child may appear 'normal' because paediatric haemoglobin thresholds are higher than adult values during early childhood.
